sections.b: In Mark, Pharisees ask whether a man may divorce his wife at all, and Jesus answers from creation: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh, so "What God has yoked together, then, no human being should separate" (Mark 10:9). In private he adds that a man who divorces and remarries commits adultery "against her," against his first wife, a phrase that treats the wife as the one wronged, and that a wife who divorces her husband and remarries does the same (Mark 10:11–12). Mark's form has no exception clause; Matthew's does (Matthew 19:9). The saying about a wife who divorces fits Roman law, where either partner could end a marriage, and speaks to Mark's readers in the Roman world.
sections.refs: Mark 10:2–12; Genesis 1:27; Genesis 2:24; Deuteronomy 24:1–4; Matthew 19:3–12; 1 Corinthians 7:10–13

common: Mark's absolute form of the divorce saying (no exception) is generally thought to be older than Matthew's.
uncommon: Some scholars think 10:12 is Jesus' own rebuke of Herodias, not Mark's application to Roman law.

sections.h: Mark: the man who had much property
sections.b: Mark tells of a man who ran up, knelt and asked how to inherit eternal life. Jesus "fixed his eyes on him and loved him," a detail only Mark gives, and told him to sell what he had, give to the poor and follow (Mark 10:21). He went away grieving, "He owned a great deal of property." Jesus' words, "With what difficulty will people who have money get into the kingdom of God!" stunned disciples who took wealth as a sign of God's blessing; the oldest manuscripts of Mark 10:24 do not soften it by adding "those who trust in riches." Salvation is possible only with God (Mark 10:27). Those who leave homes and families receive a hundredfold now, in the new family of believers, "along with persecutions" (Mark 10:30).

common: The camel and the needle's eye is a picture of the impossible, not a reference to a small city gate.
uncommon: Prosperity teachers read the "hundredfold" of Mark 10:30 as a promise of financial return.

sections.h: A ransom in place of many (Mark 10:45)
sections.b: Mark's Jesus explains his death in one sentence: "The Son of Man, too, did not come to have people serve him. He came to serve, and to give his life as a ransom in place of many" (Mark 10:45). A ransom (lutron) freed a slave or captive. Many hear Isaiah 53, where the servant gives his life as a guilt offering and bears the sin of many; others think Daniel 7 is the main background. At the Last Supper the cup is blood "poured out for many" (Mark 14:24). The scribe of Mark 12:33 adds the prophets' view that love of God and neighbor is worth more than all burnt offerings and sacrifices. Churches explain the ransom differently: see the card on Mark 10.
sections.refs: Mark 10:45; Isaiah 53:10–12; Mark 14:24; Mark 12:33; 1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6

sections.h: The Son of Man who serves
sections.b: In Daniel 7 one like a son of man receives a kingdom, and all peoples serve him. In Mark 10:45 Jesus turns the picture around: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and give his life. The third prediction (Mark 10:33–34) says the Son of Man will be handed over, condemned, mocked, whipped and killed, and rise after three days. Mark keeps both sides: the Son of Man who suffers now and the Son of Man who comes in glory (Mark 8:38; 13:26; 14:62).

Mark's first use of the word "slave" (doulos) comes in Jesus' teaching on greatness: "if anyone among you wishes to be first, he will be everyone's slave" (Mark 10:44). In the Roman world a slave was property at the bottom of the social order, and the saying overturns the ladder of honor that "those who are thought of as their rulers" climbed (Mark 10:42). In the parable of the tenants, the owner's slaves stand for the prophets (Mark 12:2–5).

Mark tells the entry plainly. The colt is one no one has ridden (Mark 11:2), fit for sacred and royal use; Mark does not quote Zechariah 9:9 as Matthew and John do. The crowd sings Psalm 118 and hails "our father David's kingdom, which is coming" (Mark 11:10). Then the scene ends quietly: Jesus enters the temple, looks around at everything, and goes out to Bethany because it is late (Mark 11:11). In Mark the action in the temple comes the next day.

sections.h: The fig tree and the temple in Mark
sections.b: Mark wraps Jesus' action in the temple inside the story of a fig tree: Jesus curses a leafy tree without fruit (Mark 11:12–14), throws out the traders and quotes Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11 (Mark 11:15–17), keeping Isaiah's words "for all the nations", and the next morning the tree is withered from the roots (Mark 11:20–21). Most scholars read the sandwich as a sign of judgment on the temple, which Jesus foretells in Mark 13:2. Only Mark says Jesus stopped people carrying things through the temple (Mark 11:16) and keeps "for all the nations." Then Jesus teaches prayer and forgiveness that do not depend on the temple (Mark 11:22–25), and the scribe agrees that love outweighs all sacrifices (Mark 12:33).
sections.refs: Mark 11:11–25; Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11; Mark 12:33; Mark 12:41–44; Mark 13:1–2

common: The temple action was the main cause of the authorities' move against Jesus (Mark 11:18).
uncommon: Some scholars think the incident was too small to be noticed in so large a court, and that Mark has enlarged its significance.

sections.b: Beside the withered fig tree Jesus says, "Have faith in God": whoever tells "this mountain" to be thrown into the sea and does not waver will have it, and whatever they pray for, they should believe they have received it (Mark 11:22–24). Spoken between the Mount of Olives and the temple mount, after the temple scene, "this mountain" may point to the temple. The past tense, "received," is the oldest reading. Mark at once ties prayer to forgiving others (Mark 11:25).

"Whenever you are standing in prayer and you have a complaint against anyone, forgive him" (Mark 11:25). Jews stood to pray, and the main synagogue prayer is still called the Standing (Amidah). Mark has no Lord's Prayer, but this saying shares its words and its link between forgiving and being forgiven. Coming right after the temple scene and Isaiah's "house of prayer for all the nations" (Mark 11:17), it points to prayer that does not depend on a building.

sections.h: The tenants of the vineyard in Mark
sections.b: Mark's parable of the tenants (Mark 12:1–12) is told to the chief priests, scribes and elders in the temple and starts from Isaiah's song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7). The owner sends slave after slave, and finally his "dearly loved son," whom the tenants kill and throw out unburied. In Mark the leaders "could tell the parable was aimed at them" (Mark 12:12). It is the one story parable in Mark told to Jesus' opponents (the short sayings of 3:23–27 also answer opponents), and the only parable in which Jesus nearly names himself.
sections.refs: Mark 12:1–12; Isaiah 5:1–7; Psalm 118:22–23; Matthew 21:33–46; Luke 20:9–19; Gospel of Thomas 65

sections.b: Pharisees and Herodians ask whether to pay the census, a tax Rome had imposed on Judea since AD 6 and the cause of Judas the Galilean's revolt. Jesus asks for a denarius, with its image of the emperor, and says, "Pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God" (Mark 12:17). Mark uses the Latin word census, and his readers lived under the emperor. Earlier, Jesus contrasted "those who are thought of as" rulers, who lord it over others, with the Son of Man who serves (Mark 10:42–45).

The Sadducees, the priestly upper class who denied the resurrection, mock it with a case from the brother-in-law's law: a woman married in turn to seven brothers. Jesus answers that they know neither the Scriptures nor God's power. The raised do not marry but are like angels; and God's words at the bush, "I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob," show that God is the God of the living. On this, Jesus sides with the Pharisees and later rabbinic teaching.

Asked for the first commandment, Mark's Jesus begins where every Jew began each morning and evening: "Listen, Israel: The Lord is our God. The Lord is one" (Mark 12:29), then the command to love God with all one's heart, being, mind and strength. Only Mark includes the opening line; Matthew and Luke give only the command to love. The scribe repeats it: "he is one, and apart from him there is no other" (Mark 12:32), echoing Deuteronomy 4:35. Jesus' answer to the rich man, "No one is good except one: God" (Mark 10:18), may echo the same creed.
sections.refs: Mark 12:29–33; Deuteronomy 6:4–5; Deuteronomy 4:35; Mark 10:18; Matthew 22:37; Luke 10:27

sections.b: In Mark the question about the greatest commandment comes from a friendly scribe. Jesus joins the Shema to Leviticus 19:18, "You are to love your neighbor as yourself," and says no other commandment ranks above these. The scribe agrees and adds that loving God and neighbor counts for more than all burnt offerings and sacrifices, and Jesus tells him he is "not far from the kingdom of God." Jewish texts before and after Jesus also joined love of God and love of neighbor (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs; Philo; Akiva in the Sifra).
sections.refs: Mark 12:28–34; Leviticus 19:18; Deuteronomy 6:4–5; 1 Samuel 15:22; Matthew 22:34–40; Luke 10:25–28

sections.b: Mark saves the title "Son of David" for the end of the road. Blind Bartimaeus is the first to cry it (Mark 10:47–48); the crowd hails "our father David's kingdom" (Mark 11:10); and in the temple Jesus asks how the Messiah can be only David's son when David, in Psalm 110:1, calls him "Lord" (Mark 12:35–37). Most readers take the riddle to mean the Messiah is David's son and more.

Jesus warns against scribes who "eat up widows' houses" while making long prayers (Mark 12:40), and then points to a poor widow who drops her last two coins, "her whole living," into the temple treasury (Mark 12:42–44). Most readers hear praise of her total giving. Others, following Addison Wright, hear a lament: the widow is the very victim of the system Jesus has just condemned, giving to a temple he is about to say will be torn down (Mark 13:2).

common: The widow's two coins are a lesson that God measures a gift by its cost.
uncommon: Jesus laments that the widow was drained by the temple system (Addison Wright, 1982).

sections.b: The Sadducees appear only once in Mark, in the temple during Jesus' last week (Mark 12:18–27). Mark introduces them by their best-known belief: "They say there is no resurrection." Their question, about a widow married in turn to seven brothers under the law of Deuteronomy 25:5–6, is meant to make the resurrection look absurd from the Torah itself. Jesus answers from the Torah too, from God's words at the bush (Exodus 3:6), and on this point stands with the Pharisees.

Jesus' last stop before Jerusalem in Mark is Jericho, where blind Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, sits begging by the road. He calls Jesus "Son of David," throws off his cloak, receives his sight and follows Jesus "on the road" up to Jerusalem (Mark 10:46–52). Herodian Jericho, a palm oasis with a royal palace, lay about 15 miles (24 kilometers) from Jerusalem and some 3,300 feet (1,000 meters) below it.
